cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors.title: No zero divisors in F[x]
cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors.title_html: No zero divisors in F[x]
cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors.html:
Let F be a field and p,q,r∈F[x].

  1. If pq=0, then p=0 or q=0.
  2. If pq=pr and p≠0, then q=r.

def-additive-inverse.title: Additive inverse
def-additive-inverse.html: The additive inverse of A∈Mm×n(F) is −A=(−1)A, with entries −aij. We write A−B=A+(−B).

def-cartesian-product.title: Cartesian product
def-cartesian-product.html: Let A and B be sets. The Cartesian product of A and B is the set of ordered pairs A×B={(a,b):a∈A, b∈B}. More generally, for sets A1,…,An, the product A1×⋯×An is the set of all ordered lists (a1,…,an) with ai∈Ai for each i.

def-characteristic.title: Characteristic
def-characteristic.html: Let F be a field. If there is a positive integer n with n⋅1=0, the characteristic of F is the smallest such n. If there is no such n, the characteristic of F is 0.

def-common-number-sets.title: Common number sets
def-common-number-sets.html:
We write

  • N={0,1,2,3,…} for the natural numbers; in this book N includes 0;
  • Z={…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…} for the integers;
  • Q for the rational numbers, the numbers a/b with a,b∈Z and b≠0;
  • R for the real numbers;
  • C for the complex numbers, studied later in this chapter.

def-complex-numbers.title: Complex Numbers
def-complex-numbers.html: The set of complex numbers is C:=R2={(a,b):a,b∈R}, with addition and multiplication defined for every (a,b),(c,d)∈C by (a,b)+(c,d):=(a+c,b+d),(a,b)(c,d):=(ac−bd,ad+bc). We write a for (a,0) and i for (0,1), so that (a,b)=a+bi. For z=a+bi with a,b∈R, the real part of z is Rez:=a and the imaginary part of z is Imz:=b.

def-composition.title: Composition
def-composition.html: Let f:X→Y and g:Y→Z be functions. The composition g∘f:X→Z is defined by (g∘f)(x):=g(f(x))for every x∈X.

def-conjugate-modulus.title: Conjugate and Modulus
def-conjugate-modulus.html: Let z=a+bi∈C with a,b∈R. The complex conjugate of z is z―:=a−bi. The modulus (or absolute value) of z is the real number |z|:=a2+b2≥0, the non-negative square root.

def-connectives.title: Negation, conjunction, disjunction
def-connectives.html:
Let P and Q be statements.

  • The negation ¬P (“not P”) is true when P is false, and false when P is true.
  • The conjunction P∧Q (“P and Q”) is true when both P and Q are true, and false otherwise.
  • The disjunction P∨Q (“P or Q”) is true when at least one of P, Q is true, and false only when both are false.

def-degree.title: Degree
def-degree.html:
Let p=∑akxk∈F[x].

  • If p≠0, the degree of p, written deg⁡p, is the largest n∈N with an≠0. The coefficient an is the leading coefficient of p, and p is monic if its leading coefficient is 1.
  • The zero polynomial has degree deg⁡0=−∞.

We use the conventions −∞<n and −∞+n=n+(−∞)=−∞ for every n∈N, and −∞+(−∞)=−∞.

def-diagonal-matrix.title: Diagonal matrix
def-diagonal-matrix.html: A square matrix A∈Mn(F) is diagonal if aij=0 whenever i≠j. We write diag(d1,…,dn) for the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries d1,…,dn.

def-divisibility-prime.title: Divisibility and primes
def-divisibility-prime.html: Let a and b be integers. We say a divides b, written a∣b, if there exists an integer k with b=ak. An integer p is prime if p≥2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p.

def-empty-set.title: Empty set
def-empty-set.html: The empty set ∅ is the set with no elements: x∉∅ for every object x.

def-equivalence-class.title: Equivalence class
def-equivalence-class.html: Let ∼ be an equivalence relation on X, and let x∈X. The equivalence class of x is [x]:={y∈X:y∼x}. Any element of [x] is called a representative of the class.

def-equivalence-relation.title: Equivalence relation
def-equivalence-relation.html:
A relation ∼ on a set X is an equivalence relation if it satisfies the following three conditions.

  1. Reflexive: x∼x for every x∈X.
  2. Symmetric: for all x,y∈X, if x∼y then y∼x.
  3. Transitive: for all x,y,z∈X, if x∼y and y∼z then x∼z.

def-field.title: Field
def-field.html:
A field is a set F together with two functions, addition +:F×F→F, (a,b)↦a+b, and multiplication ⋅:F×F→F, (a,b)↦a⋅b=ab, satisfying the following axioms.

  1. a+b=b+a for all a,b∈F.
  2. (a+b)+c=a+(b+c) for all a,b,c∈F.
  3. There exists an element 0∈F such that a+0=a for every a∈F.
  4. For every a∈F there exists an element −a∈F such that a+(−a)=0.
  5. (ab)c=a(bc) for all a,b,c∈F.
  6. ab=ba for all a,b∈F.
  7. There exists an element 1∈F with 1≠0 such that a⋅1=a for every a∈F.
  8. For every non-zero a∈F there exists an element a−1∈F such that aa−1=1.
  9. a(b+c)=ab+ac for all a,b,c∈F.

def-function.title: Function
def-function.html:
Let X and Y be sets. A function (or map) f:X→Y is a rule that assigns to every element x∈X exactly one element f(x)∈Y. The set X is the domain of f, the set Y is its codomain, and f(x) is the value of f at x. We also write x↦f(x).

Two functions f:X→Y and g:X′→Y′ are equal if X=X′, Y=Y′, and f(x)=g(x) for every x∈X.

def-group.title: Group
def-group.html:
A group is a set G together with a binary operation G×G→G, (a,b)↦ab, such that:

  1. (Associativity) (ab)c=a(bc) for all a,b,c∈G;
  2. (Identity) there is an element e∈G with ea=ae=a for every a∈G;
  3. (Inverses) for every a∈G there is b∈G with ab=ba=e, where e is the element of (G2).

The group is abelian if moreover ab=ba for all a,b∈G.

def-group-homomorphism.title: Group homomorphism
def-group-homomorphism.html: Let G and H be groups. A function φ:G→H is a homomorphism if φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) for all a,b∈G. A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism. The kernel of φ is kerφ={g∈G:φ(g)=eH}, where eH is the identity of H.

def-identity-function.title: Identity function
def-identity-function.html: For a set X, the identity function on X is idX:X→X, idX(x)=x.

def-identity-matrix.title: Identity matrix
def-identity-matrix.html: The identity matrix In∈Mn(F) has entries (In)ij=δij={1if i=j,0if i≠j. That is, 1 on the main diagonal and 0 elsewhere. We write I when the size is clear. The symbol δij is the Kronecker delta.

def-image-preimage.title: Image and preimage
def-image-preimage.html:
Let f:X→Y be a function, A⊆X and B⊆Y.

  • The image of A under f is f(A):={f(a):a∈A}⊆Y. The set f(X) is called the image of f.
  • The preimage of B under f is f−1(B):={x∈X:f(x)∈B}⊆X.

def-implication-converse-contrapositive.title: Implication, converse, contrapositive
def-implication-converse-contrapositive.html:
Let P and Q be statements.

  • The implication P⇒Q (“if P then Q”) is false when P is true and Q is false, and it is true in every other case. We call P the hypothesis and Q the conclusion.
  • The converse of P⇒Q is the implication Q⇒P.
  • The contrapositive of P⇒Q is the implication ¬Q⇒¬P.

def-indexed-family.title: Unions and intersections of indexed families
def-indexed-family.title_html: Unions and intersections of indexed families
def-indexed-family.html: Let I be a set, and for each i∈I let Ai be a set. The collection (Ai)i∈I is an indexed family of sets, with index set I. Its union is ⋃i∈IAi={x:∃i∈I:x∈Ai}, and, if I is non-empty, its intersection is ⋂i∈IAi={x:∀i∈I:x∈Ai}.

def-injective-surjective-bijective.title: Injective, surjective, bijective
def-injective-surjective-bijective.html:
Let f:X→Y be a function.

  • f is injective (one-to-one) if for all x1,x2∈X, f(x1)=f(x2) implies x1=x2.
  • f is surjective (onto) if for every y∈Y there exists x∈X with f(x)=y. Equivalently, f(X)=Y.
  • f is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

def-intersection.title: Intersection
def-intersection.html: The intersection of sets A and B is A∩B={x:x∈A and x∈B}. We call A and B disjoint if A∩B=∅.

def-inverse-function.title: Inverse function
def-inverse-function.html: Let f:X→Y. A function g:Y→X is an inverse of f if g∘f=idXandf∘g=idY. If f has an inverse, f is invertible.

def-invertible-matrix.title: Invertible matrix
def-invertible-matrix.html: A square matrix A∈Mn(F) is invertible if there exists B∈Mn(F) such that AB=InandBA=In. Such a B is called an inverse of A. A square matrix that is not invertible is called singular.

def-left-right-inverse.title: Left and right inverses
def-left-right-inverse.html: Let f:X→Y. A function g:Y→X is a left inverse of f if g∘f=idX, and a right inverse of f if f∘g=idY.

def-matrix.title: Matrix
def-matrix.html: Let F be a field and m,n≥1 integers. An m×n matrix over F is a rectangular array A=(a11a12⋯a1na21a22⋯a2n⋮⋮⋱⋮am1am2⋯amn) with m rows and n columns, whose entries aij lie in F. Formally, it is a function {1,…,m}×{1,…,n}→F, (i,j)↦aij. The set of all such matrices is Mm×n(F), and we write Mn(F)=Mn×n(F) for the square matrices.

def-matrix-addition.title: Matrix addition
def-matrix-addition.html: Let A=(aij) and B=(bij) be in Mm×n(F), of the same size. Their sum is A+B∈Mm×n(F) with (A+B)ij=aij+bij.

def-matrix-multiplication.title: Matrix multiplication
def-matrix-multiplication.html: Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F) and B=(bjk)∈Mn×p(F), so that the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. Their product is the matrix AB∈Mm×p(F) with entries (AB)ik=∑j=1naijbjk=ai1b1k+ai2b2k+⋯+ainbnk for 1≤i≤m and 1≤k≤p. If the sizes do not match, AB is not defined.

def-n-tuple.title: n-tuples
def-n-tuple.title_html: n-tuples
def-n-tuple.html: Let A be a set and n≥1 an integer. An n-tuple of elements of A is an ordered list (a1,…,an) with each ai∈A. The set of all of them is An=A×A×⋯×A⏟n factors. Two n-tuples are equal exactly when ai=bi for every i=1,…,n.

def-negation-of-quantifiers.title: Negation of quantifiers
def-negation-of-quantifiers.html:
Let P(x) be a predicate with x ranging over S. Then

¬(∀x∈S:P(x)) ≡ ∃x∈S:¬P(x),¬(∃x∈S:P(x)) ≡ ∀x∈S:¬P(x).

For a statement with several quantifiers, apply these rules from the outside in: each ∀ becomes ∃, each ∃ becomes ∀, the ranges stay the same, and the innermost condition is negated using @thm-de-morgan-logic.

def-parity.title: Even and odd
def-parity.html: An integer n is even if there exists an integer k with n=2k. An integer n is odd if there exists an integer k with n=2k+1.

def-partition.title: Partition
def-partition.html:
A partition of a set X is a collection P of subsets of X, called blocks, such that:

  1. every block is non-empty;
  2. distinct blocks are disjoint: if B,B′∈P and B≠B′, then B∩B′=∅;
  3. the blocks cover X: every x∈X lies in some block.

def-polynomial.title: Polynomial
def-polynomial.html:
Let F be a field. A polynomial over F in the indeterminate x is a sequence (a0,a1,a2,…) of elements of F, indexed by N, such that only finitely many ak are non-zero. That is, there is some N∈N with ak=0 for every k>N.

The element ak is the coefficient of xk. We write the polynomial as p=a0+a1x+a2x2+⋯+aNxN=∑k=0Nakxk. Two polynomials p=∑akxk and q=∑bkxk are equal if and only if ak=bk for every k∈N.

def-polynomial-evaluation.title: Evaluation and roots
def-polynomial-evaluation.html: Let F be a field, p=∑k=0Nakxk∈F[x] and c∈F. The value of p at c is the element p(c)=∑k=0Nakck=a0+a1c+⋯+aNcN∈F, where c0=1. An element c∈F is a root of p if p(c)=0. The function F→F, c↦p(c), is the polynomial function of p.

def-polynomial-of-matrix.title: Powers and polynomials of a matrix
def-polynomial-of-matrix.title_html: Powers and polynomials of a matrix
def-polynomial-of-matrix.html: Let A∈Mn(F). The powers of A are defined recursively by A0=In,Ak+1=AkA(k∈N). For a polynomial p=a0+a1x+⋯+aNxN∈F[x], the matrix p(A) is p(A)=a0In+a1A+a2A2+⋯+aNAN∈Mn(F).

def-polynomial-ring.title: The polynomial ring F[x]
def-polynomial-ring.title_html: The polynomial ring F[x]
def-polynomial-ring.html: Let F be a field. The set of all polynomials over F is denoted F[x]. For p=∑akxk and q=∑bkxk in F[x], define the sum p+q and the product pq by their coefficients: p+q=∑k(ak+bk)xk,pq=∑k(∑i=0kaibk−i)xk.

def-polynomials-bounded-degree.title: Polynomials of degree at most n
def-polynomials-bounded-degree.title_html: Polynomials of degree at most n
def-polynomials-bounded-degree.html: Let F be a field and n∈N. The set of polynomials over F of degree at most n is F[x]≤n={p∈F[x]:deg⁡p≤n}={a0+a1x+⋯+anxn:a0,…,an∈F}.

def-polynomials-exact-degree.title: Polynomials of degree exactly n
def-polynomials-exact-degree.title_html: Polynomials of degree exactly n
def-polynomials-exact-degree.html: Let F be a field and n∈N. The set of polynomials over F of degree exactly n is F[x]=n={p∈F[x]:deg⁡p=n}={a0+a1x+⋯+anxn:a0,…,an∈F, an≠0}.

def-power-set.title: Power set
def-power-set.html: The power set of a set S is the set of all subsets of S: P(S)={X:X⊆S}.

def-quantifiers.title: Quantifiers
def-quantifiers.html:
Let P(x) be a predicate whose variable x ranges over a fixed collection S.

  • The universal statement ∀x∈S:P(x) (“for every x in S, P(x)”) is true when P(x) is true for every element x of S, and false otherwise.
  • The existential statement ∃x∈S:P(x) (“there exists x in S such that P(x)”) is true when P(x) is true for at least one element x of S, and false otherwise.

The symbols ∀ and ∃ are the universal and existential quantifiers.

def-quotient-set.title: Quotient set
def-quotient-set.html: Let ∼ be an equivalence relation on X. The quotient set of X by ∼ is the set of all equivalence classes, X/∼:={[x]:x∈X}. The function π:X→X/∼, π(x)=[x], is the quotient map.

def-relation.title: Relation
def-relation.html: A relation on a set X is a subset R⊆X×X. When (x,y)∈R we say x is related to y and write xRy, or x∼y when the relation is fixed.

def-scalar-multiplication.title: Scalar multiplication
def-scalar-multiplication.html: Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F) and c∈F. The scalar multiple cA∈Mm×n(F) has entries (cA)ij=caij.

def-set-builder.title: Set-builder notation
def-set-builder.html: Let S be a set and let P(x) be a predicate for x∈S. The set {x∈S:P(x)} is the set whose elements are exactly those x∈S for which P(x) is true.

def-set-difference.title: Set difference and complement
def-set-difference.html: The difference of sets A and B is A∖B={x∈A:x∉B}. When all sets under discussion are subsets of one fixed set U, the complement of B⊆U is Bc=U∖B.

def-set-equality.title: Set equality
def-set-equality.html: Two sets A and B are equal, written A=B, if they have exactly the same elements: ∀x:(x∈A⇔x∈B).

def-subgroup.title: Subgroup
def-subgroup.html: Let G be a group. A subset H⊆G is a subgroup of G if e∈H, and ab∈H and a−1∈H for all a,b∈H.

def-subset.title: Subset
def-subset.html: Let A and B be sets. We say A is a subset of B, and write A⊆B, if ∀x:(x∈A⇒x∈B). If A⊆B and A≠B, then A is a proper subset of B, written A⊊B.

def-symmetric-matrix.title: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
def-symmetric-matrix.html: A square matrix A∈Mn(F) is symmetric if AT=A, that is, aij=aji for all i,j. It is skew-symmetric if AT=−A, that is, aij=−aji for all i,j.

def-trace.title: Trace
def-trace.html: The trace of a square matrix A=(aij)∈Mn(F) is the sum of its diagonal entries: trA=∑i=1naii=a11+a22+⋯+ann∈F.

def-transpose.title: Transpose
def-transpose.html: Let A=(aij)∈Mm×n(F). The transpose of A is the matrix AT∈Mn×m(F) with entries (AT)ij=aji.

def-union.title: Union
def-union.html: The union of sets A and B is A∪B={x:x∈A or x∈B}.

def-upper-triangular.title: Upper triangular matrix
def-upper-triangular.html: A square matrix A∈Mn(F) is upper triangular if aij=0 whenever i>j, that is, every entry strictly below the main diagonal is zero. It is lower triangular if aij=0 whenever i<j.

def-zero-matrix.title: Zero matrix
def-zero-matrix.html: The zero matrix 0=0m×n∈Mm×n(F) is the matrix all of whose entries are 0.

exm-equivalence-classes.title: Equivalence classes
exm-equivalence-classes.html:
1. For equality on X, [x]={x}. Every class has one element.
  2. For congruence modulo 3 on Z: [0]={…,−6,−3,0,3,6,…},[1]={…,−5,−2,1,4,7,…},[2]={…,−4,−1,2,5,8,…}. Here [0]=[3]=[−3] and [2]=[−1]: one class, many names.
  3. For “same length” on strings of a,b, the class of ab is {aa,ab,ba,bb}, and the class of the empty string contains only the empty string.
  4. For the full relation X×X on a non-empty set X, there is a single class, [x]=X.
  5. For “same distance from the origin” on R2, the class of (x,y) is the circle of radius x2+y2 centered at the origin. The class of the origin is the one-point set {(0,0)}.

exm-equivalence-relations.title: Equivalence relations

  2. Congruence modulo n on Z, for a fixed integer n≥1: a≡b(modn) if n∣a−b.
  3. “Same length” on the set S of finite strings of the letters a,b: u∼v if u and v have the same number of letters.
  4. “Same value”: for a function f:X→Y, put x∼fx′ if f(x)=f(x′).
  5. Fractions: on P=Z×(Z∖{0}), put (a,b)∼(c,d) if ad=bc.

exm-functions.title: First examples
exm-functions.html:
Check each of the following against the two clauses of @def-function.

  1. f:R→R, f(x)=3x−5. Every real x gives one real number 3x−5.
  2. s:R2→R, s(x,y)=x+y. The domain is a Cartesian product; each pair gives one sum.
  3. ℓ:{finite strings of the letters a,b}→N, sending a string to its length. The empty string has length 0, which is why it matters that N contains 0.
  4. For any set X, the rule x↦x is a function X→X. It looks too simple to matter, but it will play the role that the number 1 plays for multiplication.
  5. For any set Y, there is exactly one function ∅→Y, the empty function. Both clauses are about elements of the domain, and there are none, so they hold vacuously. It is a degenerate case that makes statements like “for every set X” true without exceptions.

exm-groups.title: Groups
exm-groups.html: Check that each of the following is a group, and decide which are abelian: (Z,+); (F,+) and (F∖{0},⋅) for a field F; GLn(F) under matrix multiplication; the set Sn of bijections {1,…,n}→{1,…,n} under composition; and a one-element set {e} with ee=e.

exm-image-preimage.title: Images and preimages of the squaring map
exm-image-preimage.title_html: Images and preimages of the squaring map
exm-image-preimage.html: Let q:R→R, q(x)=x2. Compute q([−1,2]), q−1([1,4]) and q−1([−5,−1]).

exm-indexed-families.title: Indexed unions and intersections of intervals
exm-indexed-families.title_html: Indexed unions and intersections of intervals
exm-indexed-families.html: For each integer n≥1, let An=[1/n,1] and Bn=(0,1/n). Show that ⋃n=1∞An=(0,1]and⋂n=1∞Bn=∅. You may use the fact that for every real x>0 there is an integer n≥1 with 1/n<x.

exm-injective-surjective-bijective.title: Deciding injectivity and surjectivity
exm-injective-surjective-bijective.html:
Determine which of the following functions are injective, surjective or bijective.

  1. f:R→R, f(x)=3x−5.
  2. g:Z→Z, g(n)=2n.
  3. s:R2→R, s(x,y)=x+y.
  4. idX:X→X, x↦x, for any set X.

exm-inverse-function.title: Finding inverses
exm-inverse-function.html:
For each function, decide whether it is invertible, and if so find its inverse.

  1. f:R→R, f(x)=5−2x.
  2. t:R2→R2, t(x,y)=(y,x).
  3. g:R→R, g(x)=x2.
  4. h:[0,∞)→[0,∞), h(x)=x2.

exm-inverse-matrices.title: Some invertible matrices
exm-inverse-matrices.html: Show that each of the following is invertible and find its inverse: In; a diagonal matrix D=diag(d1,…,dn) with all di≠0; A=(2153)∈M2(R); and U=(1101)∈M2(F2).

exm-matrices.title: Matrices over different fields
exm-matrices.html: Identify the size, the field and a few entries of each matrix: A=(1−20314),B=(i1+i02−i),C=(101110011),D=(5). Here C is meant over F2. Also write out the 2×2 real matrix E with eij=i+2j.

exm-matrix-addition.title: Adding and scaling
exm-matrix-addition.html: Let A=(1−20314) and B=(22−10−51) in M2×3(R). Compute A+B, 3A and A−2B.

exm-matrix-multiplication.title: A product of square matrices
exm-matrix-multiplication.html: Let A=(2−103) and B=(14−21) in M2(R). Compute AB and BA.

exm-matrix-multiplication-dimensions.title: Products of rectangular matrices
exm-matrix-multiplication-dimensions.html: Let A=(102−131)∈M2×3(R) and B=(312110)∈M3×2(R). Determine the sizes of AB and BA and compute them. Then compute (12)(34) and (34)(12).

exm-n-tuples.title: Sets of tuples
exm-n-tuples.html: Describe some elements of R2, Z3 and {0,1}3, and count the elements of {0,1}3.

exm-negation-basic.title: Negating simple quantified statements
exm-negation-basic.html:
Negate each statement, and say which of the statement and its negation is true.

  1. ∀x∈R:x2≥0.
  2. ∃n∈Z:n is even and n>10.
  3. ∀x∈R ∃y∈R:y>x.

exm-negation-injectivity.title: What “not injective” means
exm-negation-injectivity.html:
A function f from A to B is called injective if

∀a1∈A ∀a2∈A:(f(a1)=f(a2)⇒a1=a2).

Write down, with no “not” in front, what it means for f to be not injective. Then show that f(x)=x2, from R to R, is not injective.

exm-negation-not-all-zero.title: Negating “only the zero combination”
exm-negation-not-all-zero.html:
Consider the pairs (1,2), (2,4), (0,1), and the statement

∀a,b,c∈R:(a(1,2)+b(2,4)+c(0,1)=(0,0) ⇒ a=0∧b=0∧c=0).

Negate it, and decide which of the statement and its negation is true.

exm-negation-surjectivity.title: What “not surjective” means
exm-negation-surjectivity.html:
A function f from A to B is called surjective if

∀b∈B ∃a∈A:f(a)=b.

Negate this, and show that f(x)=x2, from R to R, is not surjective.

exm-nested-quantifiers.title: Swapping two quantifiers
exm-nested-quantifiers.html:
Compare the two statements

(i)  ∀x∈R ∃y∈R:y>x,(ii)  ∃y∈R ∀x∈R:y>x.

Decide which is true.

exm-non-equivalence.title: Relations that are not equivalence relations
exm-non-equivalence.title_html: Relations that are not equivalence relations
exm-non-equivalence.html:
Decide which of (E1)–(E3) each relation satisfies.

  1. ≤ on Z.
  2. On R: x∼y if |x−y|≤1.
  3. On R: x∼y if xy>0.

exm-polar-power.title: A Power via Polar Form
exm-polar-power.html: Compute (3+i)6.

exm-polynomial-of-matrix.title: Plugging a matrix into a polynomial
exm-polynomial-of-matrix.title_html: Plugging a matrix into a polynomial
exm-polynomial-of-matrix.html: Let A=(1203)∈M2(R) and p=x2−4x+3. Compute p(A) directly, and again using the factorization p=(x−1)(x−3).

exm-polynomial-product.title: A product, coefficient by coefficient
exm-polynomial-product.html: In R[x], compute (3x2−x+2)(x+1) from the definition.

exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2.title: Different polynomials, same function
exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2.html: Over F2, compare the polynomials x2+x and 0, and the polynomials x2 and x, both as polynomials and as functions F2→F2.

exm-q-sqrt2-field.title: \nQ(\sqrt{2}) Is a Field
exm-q-sqrt2-field.title_html: Q(2) Is a Field
exm-q-sqrt2-field.html: Let Q(2):={a+b2:a,b∈Q}⊆R, with the addition and multiplication of R. Show that Q(2) is a field, and find the inverse of 1+22.

exm-quadratic-solution-set.title: A solution set by double inclusion
exm-quadratic-solution-set.title_html: A solution set by double inclusion
exm-quadratic-solution-set.html: Prove that {x∈R:x2−3x+2=0}={1,2}.

exm-quantifiers.title: Quantified statements
exm-quantifiers.html:
Decide whether each statement is true.

  1. ∀x∈R:x2≥0.
  2. ∃x∈R:x2=−1.
  3. ∃n∈Z:n2=2.
  4. ∀n∈Z:n2≠2.

exm-quotient-set.title: Quotient sets
exm-quotient-set.html:
1. For an integer n≥1, the quotient of Z by congruence modulo n is written Z/nZ. Show that it has exactly n elements, namely [0],[1],…,[n−1].

  2. Describe the quotient of the set S of strings in a,b by “same length”, and of R2 by “same distance from the origin”.

exm-relations.title: Relations
exm-relations.html:
1. On Z: a≤b. The pairs (1,2) and (2,2) belong to the relation, (2,1) does not.
  2. On Z: a∣b (“a divides b”), meaning b=ka for some k∈Z. So 3∣12 and 3∣0, but 3∤5.
  3. On R: x∼y if x2+y2=1. As a subset of R×R=R2 this relation is the unit circle, so a relation can literally be a picture.
  4. On any set X: the empty relation R=∅, in which nothing is related to anything, and the full relation R=X×X, in which everything is related to everything. These two extremes are useful test cases for every property below.

exm-roots-of-unity.title: Roots of Unity
exm-roots-of-unity.html: Let n≥1 be an integer. Find all z∈C with zn=1, and draw them for n=6.

exm-row-equivalence.title: Row equivalence
exm-row-equivalence.html: For A,B∈Mm×n(F), say A is row equivalent to B if there is an invertible E∈Mm(F) with B=EA. Prove that row equivalence is an equivalence relation on Mm×n(F). Then, with E=(10−21), compute EA for A=(121250) and describe what E did to the rows of A.

exm-set-builder.title: Reading set-builder notation
exm-set-builder.html:
Describe each set more simply.

  1. {x∈R:x2<4}.
  2. {x∈Z:x2<4}.
  3. {n∈Z:n is even} and {2k:k∈Z}.
  4. {(x,y):x,y∈R, x+y=1}, a set of ordered pairs (made precise under Cartesian products below).

exm-set-operations.title: Operations on finite sets
exm-set-operations.html: Let A={1,2,3,4} and B={3,4,5,6}. Compute A∪B, A∩B, A∖B and B∖A.

exm-set-operations-intervals.title: Operations on intervals
exm-set-operations-intervals.html: Let A=[0,2] and B=[1,3]. Compute A∪B, A∩B and A∖B.

exm-similarity.title: Similarity
exm-similarity.html: For A,B∈Mn(F), say A is similar to B, written A∼B, if there is an invertible P∈Mn(F) with B=P−1AP. Prove that similarity is an equivalence relation on Mn(F). Then check that A=(1203) is similar to diag(1,3) using P=(1101), and show that diag(1,2) is not similar to I2 over R.

exm-special-matrices.title: Diagonal and triangular
exm-special-matrices.html: Classify each matrix as diagonal, upper triangular, lower triangular, or none of these: P=(3000−10000),Q=(123045006),R=(123045076).

exm-subsets.title: Subsets
exm-subsets.html:
Decide whether each inclusion holds.

  1. N⊆Z⊆Q⊆R.
  2. {1,2}⊆{1,2,3} and {1,4}⊆{1,2,3}.
  3. A⊆A and ∅⊆A, for any set A.
  4. {x∈R:x2=1}⊆Z.

exm-three-views.title: One product, three ways
exm-three-views.html: Let A=(123−104)∈M3×2(R),B=(21−11)∈M2(R),x=(2−1). Compute Ax as a combination of the columns of A. Then compute AB by columns, check one row by the row view, and check one entry by the entry formula.

exm-trace.title: Computing traces
exm-trace.html: Compute trA for A=(27−10−35416)∈M3(R), and trIn over R and over F2.

exm-transpose.title: Transposes, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
exm-transpose.html: Compute the transpose of A=(1−20314). Decide whether S=(123245356),K=(02−1−2031−30),S′=(123245366) over R are symmetric or skew-symmetric.

exm-vacuous-truth.title: A vacuously true implication
exm-vacuous-truth.html: Let n be an integer. Is the statement “if n is odd and n is even, then n=7” true?

exm-zero-identity.title: Zero and identity matrices
exm-zero-identity.html: Write out 02×3, I2 and I3. Which of them are diagonal?

exr-complex-numbers-a1.title: A1
exr-complex-numbers-a1.html:
1. Define the complex conjugate z― and the modulus |z| of z=a+bi, where a,b∈R.
  2. State the triangle inequality for complex numbers.
  3. True or false: |z+w|=|z|+|w| for all z,w∈C. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: zz― is a non-negative real number for every z∈C. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if z,w∈C and z2=w2, then z=w. Justify your answer.
  6. State the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

exr-complex-numbers-b1.title: B1: Arithmetic
exr-complex-numbers-b1.html:
Write each of the following in the form a+bi with a,b∈R, or as a real number where indicated.

  1. (3−2i)(4+i).
  2. 1+2i2−i.
  3. |(3+4i)(5−12i)|, without expanding the product.
  4. Re11+i and Im11+i.

exr-complex-numbers-b2.title: B2: A Square Root
exr-complex-numbers-b2.html:
1. Find all w∈C with w2=−3+4i.
  2. Hence solve z2+2z+4−4i=0.

Hint: for (b), complete the square.

exr-complex-numbers-b3.title: B3
exr-complex-numbers-b3.html: Let z∈C with z≠0. Prove that 1z=z― if and only if |z|=1.

exr-complex-numbers-b4.title: B4: Polar Form
exr-complex-numbers-b4.html:
1. Compute (1−3i)6.
  2. Find all z∈C with z3=−8i, in the form a+bi.

exr-complex-numbers-c1.title: C1: Reverse Triangle Inequality
exr-complex-numbers-c1.html:
Prove that ||z|−|w||≤|z−w| for all z,w∈C.

Hint: write z=(z−w)+w.

exr-complex-numbers-c2.title: C2: Roots of Unity Sum to Zero
exr-complex-numbers-c2.title_html: C2: Roots of Unity Sum to Zero
exr-complex-numbers-c2.html:
Let n≥2 and ω=e2πi/n.

  1. Prove that 1+ω+ω2+⋯+ωn−1=0.
  2. Deduce that ∑k=0n−1cos⁡2πkn=0 and ∑k=0n−1sin⁡2πkn=0.

Hint: compare S with ωS, where S is the sum in (a).

exr-complex-numbers-c3.title: C3: Symmetries of \nC Fixing \nR
exr-complex-numbers-c3.title_html: C3: Symmetries of C Fixing R
exr-complex-numbers-c3.html:
Let σ:C→C be a function with σ(z+w)=σ(z)+σ(w) and σ(zw)=σ(z)σ(w) for all z,w∈C, and σ(a)=a for every a∈R.

  1. Prove that σ(i)2=−1.
  2. Prove that the only complex numbers u with u2=−1 are i and −i.
  3. Deduce that either σ(z)=z for every z∈C, or σ(z)=z― for every z∈C.
  4. Show that z↦z― does satisfy all three conditions on σ.

Hint: for (b), write u=x+yi and compare real and imaginary parts.

exr-fields-a1.title: A1
exr-fields-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a set F with two operations to be a field.
  2. True or false: in every field, a2=0 implies a=0. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: Z/8Z is a field. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: in every field, 1+1≠0. Justify your answer.
  5. What are the characteristics of C and of F7?
  6. The set N with the usual addition and multiplication is not a field. Name two axioms that fail, each with a witness.

exr-fields-b1.title: B1: The Remaining Basic Properties
exr-fields-b1.html:
Let F be a field and a,b,c∈F. Using only the axioms and the parts of @thm-field-basic-properties proved in the text, prove:

  1. the element 1 in (F7) is unique;
  2. if ab=ac and a≠0, then b=c;
  3. for a≠0, the inverse a−1 is unique;
  4. (−1)a=−a.

Hint: for (d), show that a+(−1)a=0.

exr-fields-b2.title: B2: Solving Equations in \nF_7
exr-fields-b2.title_html: B2: Solving Equations in F7
exr-fields-b2.html:
1. Solve 3x+5=2 in F7.
  2. Solve the system x+2y=3, 3x+y=1 over F7.

exr-fields-b3.title: B3: Which Are Fields?
exr-fields-b3.html:
Determine which of the following are fields, with the stated operations. Justify your answer.

  1. Z/9Z, with the operations of @exm-finite-fields.
  2. Q(i):={a+bi:a,b∈Q}, with the operations of C.
  3. {a+bi:a,b∈Z}, with the operations of C.
  4. F5.

exr-fields-c1.title: C1: A Field with Four Elements
exr-fields-c1.title_html: C1: A Field with Four Elements
exr-fields-c1.html:
Let F={a+bα:a,b∈F2}, a set of four formal symbols 0,1,α,β, where β:=1+α. Define (a+bα)+(c+dα):=(a+c)+(b+d)α,(a+bα)(c+dα):=(ac+bd)+(ad+bc+bd)α, with all coefficient arithmetic in F2. (The product is what expanding gives if we replace α2 by α+1.)

  1. Write out the addition and multiplication tables of F.
  2. Prove that F is a field.
  3. Explain why there is no bijection φ:F→Z/4Z with φ(x+y)=φ(x)+φ(y) and φ(xy)=φ(x)φ(y) for all x,y∈F. So this four-element field is not “Z/4Z in disguise”.

Hint: for (c), look for a non-zero element of Z/4Z whose square is zero.

exr-fields-c2.title: C2: Finite Fields Have Prime Characteristic
exr-fields-c2.title_html: C2: Finite Fields Have Prime Characteristic
exr-fields-c2.html:
1. Let F be a finite field. Prove that the characteristic of F is a prime p.
  2. Let F be a field of characteristic p>0. Prove that p⋅a=0 for every a∈F.

Hint: for (a), the elements 1⋅1,2⋅1,3⋅1,… cannot all be different.

exr-fields-c3.title: C3: The Frobenius Identity
exr-fields-c3.html:
Let p be a prime.

  1. Let a,b∈Z with p dividing ab. Prove that p divides a or p divides b.
  2. Deduce that p divides the binomial coefficient (pk) for 0<k<p.
  3. Let F be a field of characteristic p. Prove that (x+y)p=xp+yp for all x,y∈F.

You may use the binomial theorem (x+y)n=∑k=0n(nk)⋅(xkyn−k) in any field, with integer multiples as in @lem-integer-multiples; its inductive proof uses only the field axioms.

Hint: for (a), use @lem-bezout-integers. For (b), use p!=(pk)k!(p−k)!.

exr-functions-a1.title: A1
exr-functions-a1.html:
1. State what it means for f:X→Y to be injective, and what it means to be surjective.
  2. True or false: the functions R→R, x↦x3 and R→R, x↦x⋅x⋅x are equal. Give a reason.
  3. True or false: if g∘f is injective, then g is injective. Give a reason.
  4. Write down the first line of a proof that a function f is injective, and the first line of a proof that it is surjective.
  5. True or false: the preimage f−1(B) is defined only when f is bijective.
  6. True or false: every injective function {1,2,3}→{1,2,3} is bijective. Name the result you use.

exr-functions-b1.title: B1: Injective or surjective?
exr-functions-b1.html:
Determine whether each function is injective, and whether it is surjective. Justify your answers.

  1. f:Z→Z, f(n)=3n+1.
  2. g:R2→R2, g(x,y)=(x+y,x−y).
  3. h:N→N, h(n)=⌊n/2⌋, the largest integer not exceeding n/2.
  4. p:R→R2, p(t)=(t,t2).

exr-functions-b2.title: B2: Inverses
exr-functions-b2.html:
1. Show that f:R→R, f(x)=7−4x, is invertible and find f−1.
  2. Let D=R∖{1} and define k:D→D by k(x)=x+1x−1. Show that k really takes values in D, and that k∘k=idD. Hence deduce that k is bijective and find k−1.
  3. With g as in B1(b), find g−1. Hence find the inverse of g∘g without computing g∘g first.

exr-functions-b3.title: B3: Images of unions and intersections
exr-functions-b3.title_html: B3: Images of unions and intersections
exr-functions-b3.html:
Let f:X→Y and A1,A2⊆X.

  1. Prove that f(A1∪A2)=f(A1)∪f(A2).
  2. Prove that f(A1∩A2)⊆f(A1)∩f(A2).
  3. Using q(x)=x2 on R, give an example where the inclusion in (b) is strict.

exr-functions-c1.title: C1: Left inverses are not unique
exr-functions-c1.title_html: C1: Left inverses are not unique
exr-functions-c1.html:
1. Let f:X→Y be injective but not surjective, with X having at least two elements. Prove that f has at least two different left inverses.
  2. Find two different left inverses of f:N→N, f(n)=n+1.
  3. Explain why a bijective function has exactly one left inverse.

Hint for (a): look at the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective and ask where it made a free choice.

exr-functions-c2.title: C2: Self-maps of finite and infinite sets
exr-functions-c2.title_html: C2: Self-maps of finite and infinite sets
exr-functions-c2.html:
1. Let X be a finite set and f:X→X injective. Prove that f is bijective.
  2. Show that (a) fails for X=N: give an injective f:N→N that is not bijective.
  3. Give a surjective h:N→N that is not bijective.
  4. Let X be finite and f,g:X→X with g∘f=idX. Prove that f∘g=idX as well.

Hint for (d): first show that f is bijective.

exr-functions-c3.title: C3: When images and preimages undo each other
exr-functions-c3.title_html: C3: When images and preimages undo each other
exr-functions-c3.html:
Let f:X→Y.

  1. Prove that f(f−1(B))=B for every B⊆Y if and only if f is surjective.
  2. Prove that f−1(f(A))=A for every A⊆X if and only if f is injective.

Hint: for each direction you need only one well-chosen set; try a one-element set.

exr-groups-a1.title: A1
exr-groups-a1.html:
1. State the three axioms of a group.
  2. Is Z with the operation (a,b)↦a−b a group? Justify your answer.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “in every group, (ab)−1=a−1b−1.” Justify your answer.
  4. Compute (1 3)(1 2 3) in S3.
  5. Explain why {A∈M2(R):A is not invertible} is not a subgroup of GL2(R).

exr-groups-b1.title: B1: The table of S_3
exr-groups-b1.title_html: B1: The table of S3
exr-groups-b1.html: List the six elements of S3 in cycle notation and write out the table whose entry in row x and column y is xy. Hence find all elements x∈S3 with x2=id, and all x that commute with every element of S3.

exr-groups-b2.title: B2: Invertible upper triangular matrices
exr-groups-b2.html:
Let F be a field and T={(ab0d):a,b,d∈F, a≠0, d≠0}.

  1. Prove that T is a subgroup of GL2(F).
  2. For which fields F is T abelian? Justify your answer.

exr-groups-b3.title: B3: The exponential is an isomorphism
exr-groups-b3.title_html: B3: The exponential is an isomorphism
exr-groups-b3.html: Let R>0={x∈R:x>0}. Show that (R>0,⋅) is a group, and that exp:(R,+)→(R>0,⋅), x↦ex, is an isomorphism. What is its kernel? You may use the familiar facts ex+y=exey, ex>0, and that ln:R>0→R satisfies ln⁡(ex)=x and eln⁡y=y.

exr-groups-c1.title: C1: Every element its own inverse
exr-groups-c1.title_html: C1: Every element its own inverse
exr-groups-c1.html:
1. Let G be a group in which g2=gg=e for every g∈G. Prove that G is abelian.
  2. Show that (M2(F2),+) is an example of such a group, written additively.

exr-groups-c2.title: C2: The order of a product of disjoint cycles
exr-groups-c2.title_html: C2: The order of a product of disjoint cycles
exr-groups-c2.html:
The order of σ∈Sn is the smallest integer m≥1 with σm=id, where σm is the product of m copies of σ. Two cycles are disjoint if no element appears in both.

  1. Let σ=(i1 ⋯ ik) be a k-cycle. Prove that σm=id if and only if k divides m. Deduce that σ has order k.
  2. Prove that disjoint cycles σ and τ commute, and deduce (στ)m=σmτm for all m≥1.
  3. Let σ be a k-cycle and τ an l-cycle, disjoint. Prove that στ has order lcm(k,l).
  4. Find the order of (1 2)(3 4 5)∈S5.

Hint for (c): σm moves only elements that appear in σ.

exr-logic-a1.title: A1
exr-logic-a1.html:
1. Decide whether each statement is true: (i) “3<2 or 3 is odd”; (ii) “if 3<2, then 3=5”; (iii) “if 3 is odd, then 3<2”.
  2. Write the converse and the contrapositive of “if an integer n is divisible by 4, then n is even”. Which of the three statements are true for every integer n?
  3. Negate ∀x∈R ∃n∈Z:n>x, with no ¬ in front. Which of the statement and its negation is true?
  4. True or false: ¬(P∧Q)≡¬P∧¬Q for all statements P,Q. Give a reason.

exr-logic-b1.title: B1: Negating definitions
exr-logic-b1.html:
Write the negation of each definition as a quantified statement with no ¬ in front, and then say it in words.

  1. A function f from R to R is bounded if ∃M∈R ∀x∈R:|f(x)|≤M.
  2. A function f from A to B is injective if ∀a1,a2∈A:(a1≠a2⇒f(a1)≠f(a2)). Compare your answer with @exm-negation-injectivity.
  3. “Every pair of reals is a combination of (1,0) and (1,1)”: ∀p,q∈R ∃a,b∈R:(p,q)=a(1,0)+b(1,1), where pairs are added and scaled entry by entry.

exr-logic-b2.title: B2: Integers versus reals
exr-logic-b2.html:
For each statement, decide whether it is true when x and y range over Z, and whether it is true when they range over R. Justify your answer.

  1. ∀x ∃y:x<y<x+1.
  2. ∀x (x≠0⇒∃y:xy=1).
  3. ∃x ∀y:xy=y.
  4. ∀x ∃y:y2=x.

exr-logic-c1.title: C1: Exporting a hypothesis
exr-logic-c1.html: Prove that P⇒(Q⇒R) is logically equivalent to (P∧Q)⇒R for all statements P,Q,R. Explain in one sentence why this lets a theorem with two hypotheses be stated either way.

exr-logic-c2.title: C2: When can a converse fail too?
exr-logic-c2.title_html: C2: When can a converse fail too?
exr-logic-c2.html:
1. Determine whether there exist statements P and Q such that both P⇒Q and its converse Q⇒P are false. Justify your answer.
  2. Give predicates P(n) and Q(n) about integers such that both ∀n∈Z:(P(n)⇒Q(n)) and ∀n∈Z:(Q(n)⇒P(n)) are false.
  3. Explain why (a) and (b) do not contradict each other.

exr-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-matrices-a1.html:
1. Let A∈M2×3(F) and B∈M3×4(F). Which of AB, BA, ATA and BTAT are defined? Give the size of each one that is.
  2. Define what it means for A∈Mn(F) to be invertible.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if A,B∈Mn(F) and AB=0, then A=0 or B=0.” Justify your answer.
  4. Determine whether the following statement is true: “(A+B)(A−B)=A2−B2 for all A,B∈M2(R).” Justify your answer.
  5. Let A∈M3(F) have columns a1,a2,a3. Express A(2,0,−1) and the second column of A2 in terms of the columns of A and A itself.

exr-matrices-b1.title: B1: Products and sizes
exr-matrices-b1.html:
Let A=(1−12031),B=(211004),C=(1234) over R.

  1. Compute AB and BA.
  2. Determine which of AC and CA is defined, and compute it.
  3. Compute Ax for x=(2,0,−1) as a combination of the columns of A.

exr-matrices-b2.title: B2: Traces of products
exr-matrices-b2.html:
1. With A and B as in @exr-matrices-b1, verify that tr(AB)=tr(BA), although AB and BA have different sizes.
  2. Let A=diag(1,2), B=(0100) and C=(0010). Show that tr(ABC)≠tr(BAC), and verify that tr(ABC)=tr(CAB).

exr-matrices-b3.title: B3: Inverses of 2 \times 2 matrices
exr-matrices-b3.title_html: B3: Inverses of 2×2 matrices
exr-matrices-b3.html:
1. Find the inverse of (3423)∈M2(R), and check both products.
  2. Show that A=(2613) is not invertible by finding a non-zero x with Ax=0.
  3. Find the inverse of (1234)∈M2(F5).
  4. For which t∈R is (t22t) invertible?

exr-matrices-b4.title: B4: Transposes of products
exr-matrices-b4.html:
1. Prove that (A1A2⋯Ak)T=AkT⋯A2TA1T for all k≥1 and matrices A1,…,Ak whose sizes allow the product.
  2. Let A∈Mn(F). Prove that A+AT is symmetric and A−AT is skew-symmetric.

exr-matrices-c1.title: C1: AB - BA = I is impossible, or is it?
exr-matrices-c1.title_html: C1: AB−BA=I is impossible, or is it?
exr-matrices-c1.html:
1. Prove that there are no A,B∈Mn(R), for any n≥1, with AB−BA=In.
  2. Show that the argument of (a) breaks down in M2(F2), and that A=(0010), B=(0100) satisfy AB−BA=I2 over F2.

Hint: consider the trace of both sides.

exr-matrices-c2.title: C2: Triangular matrices with non-zero diagonal
exr-matrices-c2.title_html: C2: Triangular matrices with non-zero diagonal
exr-matrices-c2.html:
Let F be a field.

  1. Let U=(ab0d) with a,d≠0. Show that U is invertible and that U−1 is upper triangular.
  2. Let U=(abc0de00f) with a,d,f≠0. Show that V=(a−1−b(ad)−1(be−cd)(adf)−10d−1−e(df)−100f−1) is the inverse of U.
  3. Explain how the entries of V can be found, column by column, by solving Uvk=ek.

The general case, for all n, follows from the methods of Chapter 2.

exr-matrices-c3.title: C3: Matrices that commute
exr-matrices-c3.html:
Let N=(0100)∈M2(R).

  1. Find all X∈M2(R) with XN=NX.
  2. Deduce that the only matrices X∈M2(R) with XY=YX for every Y∈M2(R) are the scalar multiples cI2, c∈R.

exr-polynomials-a1.title: A1
exr-polynomials-a1.html:
1. Define the degree of a polynomial over a field F, including the zero polynomial. State the formula for deg⁡(pq).
  2. Is 1+x+x2+x3+⋯, with every coefficient equal to 1, a polynomial over R? Justify your answer.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “for all p,q∈F[x], deg⁡(p+q)=max(deg⁡p,deg⁡q).” Justify your answer.
  4. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if p∈F2[x] and p(c)=0 for every c∈F2, then p=0.” Justify your answer.
  5. Explain why F[x]=2 is not closed under addition, while F[x]≤2 is.

exr-polynomials-b1.title: B1: Sums, products and degrees
exr-polynomials-b1.html:
1. In R[x], let p=2x3−x+4 and q=−2x3+x2+3. Compute p+q and pq, and give their degrees. Which inequality or formula from this section does each degree illustrate?
  2. In F3[x], compute (x+2)(x2+x+1). Hence find all roots in F3 of the product.

exr-polynomials-b2.title: B2: Degree of a composition
exr-polynomials-b2.html:
For p=∑k=0makxk and q in F[x], define the composition p∘q=∑k=0makqk∈F[x], where q0=1.

  1. Prove that if p and q are non-constant, then deg⁡(p∘q)=deg⁡p⋅deg⁡q.
  2. Give an example showing the formula fails when q is constant.

Hint: first find deg⁡(qk).

exr-polynomials-b3.title: B3: All small polynomials over \nF_2
exr-polynomials-b3.title_html: B3: All small polynomials over F2
exr-polynomials-b3.html: List all polynomials in F2[x]≤2. For each, give its degree and its polynomial function (the values at 0 and 1). Hence determine which of them define the zero function, and explain why every function F2→F2 is the polynomial function of exactly two of them.

exr-polynomials-c1.title: C1: Roots of a quadratic
exr-polynomials-c1.html:
Let F be a field.

  1. Let p=ax2+bx+c∈F[x] and r∈F with p(r)=0. Prove that p=(x−r)(ax+(b+ar)).
  2. Deduce that a non-zero polynomial in F[x]≤2 has at most 2 roots in F.
  3. The same definitions make sense with coefficients in Z/8Z. Show that x2−1 has four roots there, and name the step of (b) that breaks.

Hint for (b): use (a) together with @thm-evaluation-respects-operations.

exr-polynomials-c2.title: C2: A non-zero polynomial vanishing everywhere
exr-polynomials-c2.title_html: C2: A non-zero polynomial vanishing everywhere
exr-polynomials-c2.html:
Let p be a prime and F=Fp.

  1. Fix a∈F∖{0}. Prove that the map F∖{0}→F∖{0}, b↦ab, is a bijection.
  2. Deduce that ap−1=1 for every a∈F∖{0}.
  3. Hence show that the polynomial xp−x∈Fp[x] is not the zero polynomial but that its polynomial function is the zero function.

Hint for (b): multiply together all the elements of F∖{0} in two ways.

exr-polynomials-c3.title: C3: Which polynomials have inverses?
exr-polynomials-c3.html:
1. Let F be a field and p,q∈F[x] with pq=1. Prove that p and q are non-zero constants.
  2. Show that (a) fails with coefficients in Z/4Z by computing (2x+1)2 there.

exr-proofs-a1.title: A1
exr-proofs-a1.html:
For each statement, name the proof technique you would use first (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, induction, or counterexample), and give a one-sentence reason. Then carry out the proof or refutation.

  1. The sum of two odd integers is even.
  2. For every integer n, if 3n+2 is odd, then n is odd.
  3. For every integer n≥1, 3∣4n−1.
  4. For every integer n≥1, n2≥2n.
  5. There is no largest integer.

exr-proofs-b1.title: B1: Contrapositive
exr-proofs-b1.html: Prove that for every integer n, if n2 is odd, then n is odd.

exr-proofs-b2.title: B2: Induction
exr-proofs-b2.html: Prove that for every integer n≥1, the sum of the first n odd numbers is n2: 1+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n2.

exr-proofs-b3.title: B3: \sqrt{3} is irrational
exr-proofs-b3.title_html: B3: 3 is irrational
exr-proofs-b3.html:
You may use the school fact that every integer has exactly one of the forms 3k, 3k+1, 3k+2 with k an integer.

  1. Prove that for every integer n, if 3∣n2 then 3∣n.
  2. Hence prove that there is no rational number whose square is 3.

exr-proofs-c1.title: C1: Stamps of 4 and 5
exr-proofs-c1.html:
1. Show that each of 12,13,14,15 can be written as 4a+5b with a,b∈N.
  2. Prove by strong induction that every integer n≥12 can be written as 4a+5b with a,b∈N.
  3. Show that 11 cannot be written in this form, so the bound 12 in (b) cannot be lowered to 11.

Hint: for n≥16, look at n−4.

exr-proofs-c2.title: C2: Division with remainder
exr-proofs-c2.html:
Let a and b be integers with b≥1. Let R be the collection of all non-negative integers of the form a−qb with q an integer.

  1. Show that R is non-empty.
  2. Let r be the least element of R, which exists by @thm-well-ordering, and write r=a−qb. Prove that 0≤r<b.
  3. Prove that the pair (q,r) is unique: if a=qb+r=q′b+r′ with 0≤r<b and 0≤r′<b, then q=q′ and r=r′.

Hint for (a): try q=−|a|.

exr-relations-a1.title: A1
exr-relations-a1.html:
1. State the three conditions for a relation ∼ on X to be an equivalence relation.
  2. True or false: a symmetric and transitive relation is automatically reflexive. Give a reason.
  3. True or false: if two equivalence classes [a] and [b] have an element in common, then a∼b.
  4. You want to define a function on X/∼ by a formula in a representative x. What must you check?
  5. How many elements does Z/5Z have? Is [12]=[−3] in Z/5Z?

exr-relations-b1.title: B1: Which are equivalence relations?
exr-relations-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are equivalence relations. For those that are, describe the equivalence classes. For those that are not, name a condition that fails with a specific witness.

  1. On Z: a∼b if a+b is even.
  2. On Z: a∼b if a−b is odd.
  3. On R: x∼y if x−y∈Z.
  4. On {1,2,3,…}: m∼n if m and n have a common divisor greater than 1.
  5. On the set of all subsets of {1,2,3}: A∼B if A and B have the same number of elements.

exr-relations-b2.title: B2: Parallel lines as classes
exr-relations-b2.html:
On R2, define (x,y)∼(x′,y′) if x−y=x′−y′.

  1. Prove that ∼ is an equivalence relation.
  2. Describe the class of (x0,y0) geometrically, and draw several classes.
  3. Show that [(x,y)]↦x−y is a well-defined function R2/∼→R, and that it is a bijection.

exr-relations-b3.title: B3: Multiplication modulo n
exr-relations-b3.title_html: B3: Multiplication modulo n
exr-relations-b3.html:
Fix an integer n≥1.

  1. Prove that [a][b]:=[ab] is a well-defined operation on Z/nZ.
  2. Write out the multiplication table of Z/4Z, using the representatives 0,1,2,3.
  3. Hence find a class [a]≠[0] in Z/4Z with [a][a]=[0].

exr-relations-c1.title: C1: Squares and powers modulo n
exr-relations-c1.title_html: C1: Squares and powers modulo n
exr-relations-c1.html:
1. Let n≥1. Prove that [x]↦[x2] is a well-defined function Z/nZ→Z/nZ.
  2. On N, let ≡3 be congruence modulo 3. Show that the rule [x]↦[2x]3 does not define a function from N/≡3 to Z/3Z.
  3. On N, let ≡2 be congruence modulo 2. Prove that [x]↦[2x]3 does define a function from N/≡2 to Z/3Z.

Hint for (c): compute 22 modulo 3.

exr-relations-c2.title: C2: Counting equivalence relations
exr-relations-c2.html:
1. List all partitions of {1,2,3}.
  2. Hence deduce that there are exactly 5 equivalence relations on {1,2,3}.
  3. Write the equivalence relation corresponding to the partition {{1,3},{2}} as a subset of {1,2,3}×{1,2,3}.

exr-relations-c3.title: C3: Intersections and unions of equivalence relations
exr-relations-c3.title_html: C3: Intersections and unions of equivalence relations
exr-relations-c3.html:
Let R1 and R2 be equivalence relations on a set X, viewed as subsets of X×X.

  1. Prove that R1∩R2 is an equivalence relation on X.
  2. Show by an example that R1∪R2 need not be an equivalence relation. Which condition fails?
  3. For congruence modulo 2 and modulo 3 on Z, identify R1∩R2 as a familiar relation.

Hint for (b): try congruence modulo 2 and modulo 3 on Z.

exr-sets-a1.title: A1
exr-sets-a1.html:
Decide whether each statement is true or false. Give a one-line reason.

  1. 0∈N.
  2. ∅∈∅.
  3. ∅⊆∅.
  4. {0}=∅.
  5. {1,2}={2,1,1} and (1,2)=(2,1).
  6. {1}∈P({1,2}) and {1}⊆P({1,2}).

exr-sets-b1.title: B1: The second De Morgan law
exr-sets-b1.title_html: B1: The second De Morgan law
exr-sets-b1.html: Let A, B, C be sets. Prove that A∖(B∩C)=(A∖B)∪(A∖C), which is part (b) of @thm-de-morgan-sets.

exr-sets-b2.title: B2: A distributive law
exr-sets-b2.html: Let A, B, C be sets. Prove that A∩(B∪C)=(A∩B)∪(A∩C), which is part (a) of @thm-distributive-sets.

exr-sets-b3.title: B3: An indexed intersection
exr-sets-b3.html: Prove that ⋂n=1∞(−1n,1n)={0}. You may use the fact that for every real x>0 there is an integer n≥1 with 1/n<x.

exr-sets-c1.title: C1: When union equals intersection
exr-sets-c1.html: Let A and B be sets. Prove that A∪B=A∩B if and only if A=B.

exr-sets-c2.title: C2: Counting subsets
exr-sets-c2.html:
For a finite set S, write |S| for its number of elements. The aim is to prove that |P(S)|=2|S| for every finite set S.

  1. Check the claim when S=∅.
  2. Let S have n+1 elements, fix s∈S, and let S′=S∖{s}. Show that every subset X of S belongs to exactly one of the two collections: the subsets of S with s∉X, and the subsets of S with s∈X.
  3. Show that the subsets of S with s∉X are exactly the subsets of S′, and that X↦X∖{s} and T↦T∪{s} pair off the subsets of S containing s with the subsets of S′, each undoing the other.
  4. Hence prove the claim by induction on n=|S|.

Hint: in (c), use double inclusion to check that (X∖{s})∪{s}=X when s∈X.

lem-bezout-integers.title: Bézout’s Lemma for Integers
lem-bezout-integers.html: Let a,n∈Z with n≥1, and suppose that the only positive integer dividing both a and n is 1. Then there exist x,y∈Z with ax+ny=1.

lem-classes-equal-or-disjoint.title: Classes are equal or disjoint
lem-classes-equal-or-disjoint.html:
Let ∼ be an equivalence relation on X, and let a,b∈X.

  1. [a]=[b] if and only if a∼b.
  2. Either [a]=[b] or [a]∩[b]=∅.

lem-integer-multiples.title: Integer Multiples
lem-integer-multiples.html: Let F be a field, a∈F and m,k∈N. Then (m⋅1)+(k⋅1)=(m+k)⋅1,(m⋅1)(k⋅1)=(mk)⋅1,(m⋅1)a=m⋅a.

prp-complex-arithmetic-laws.title: Arithmetic Laws in \nC
prp-complex-arithmetic-laws.title_html: Arithmetic Laws in C
prp-complex-arithmetic-laws.html:
For all z,w,u∈C:

  1. z+w=w+z and zw=wz;
  2. (z+w)+u=z+(w+u) and (zw)u=z(wu);
  3. z(w+u)=zw+zu;
  4. z+0=z, z⋅1=z, and z+(−z)=0, where −(a+bi):=(−a)+(−b)i.

prp-complex-inverse.title: Inverse of a Complex Number
prp-complex-inverse.html: Let z∈C with z≠0. Then w:=1|z|2z― satisfies zw=1. We write z−1 or 1z for this w.

prp-even-iff-square-even.title: Parity of a square
prp-even-iff-square-even.html: For every integer n, n is even if and only if n2 is even.

prp-identity-element-unique.title: Uniqueness of the identity
prp-identity-element-unique.html: Let ∗ be a binary operation on S. Then ∗ has at most one identity element.

prp-image-preimage-inclusions.title: Image and preimage inclusions
prp-image-preimage-inclusions.html: Let f:X→Y, A⊆X and B⊆Y. Then f(f−1(B))⊆BandA⊆f−1(f(A)).

prp-n-squared-plus-n-even.title: n^2 + n is even
prp-n-squared-plus-n-even.title_html: n2+n is even
prp-n-squared-plus-n-even.html: For every integer n, the integer n2+n is even.

prp-power-of-two.title: 2^n > n
prp-power-of-two.title_html: 2n>n
prp-power-of-two.html: For every natural number n, we have 2n>n.

prp-prime-factor.title: Existence of a prime factor
prp-prime-factor.html: Every integer n≥2 has a prime divisor.

prp-square-even.title: Even squares
prp-square-even.html: For every integer n, if n2 is even, then n is even.

prp-sum-first-n.title: Sum of the first n integers
prp-sum-first-n.title_html: Sum of the first n integers
prp-sum-first-n.html: For every integer n≥1, 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)2.

prp-sum-of-evens.title: Sum of even integers
prp-sum-of-evens.html: For all integers m and n, if m and n are even, then m+n is even.

thm-bijective-iff-invertible.title: Bijective if and only if invertible
thm-bijective-iff-invertible.title_html: Bijective if and only if invertible
thm-bijective-iff-invertible.html: A function f:X→Y is invertible if and only if it is bijective. Moreover, an inverse of f, when it exists, is unique; we denote it f−1:Y→X.

thm-characteristic-prime.title: The Characteristic Is 0 or Prime
thm-characteristic-prime.title_html: The Characteristic Is 0 or Prime
thm-characteristic-prime.html: The characteristic of a field is either 0 or a prime number.

thm-complex-triangle-inequality.title: Triangle Inequality
thm-complex-triangle-inequality.html: For all z,w∈C, |z+w|≤|z|+|w|.

thm-composition-associative.title: Associativity of composition
thm-composition-associative.html: Let f:X→Y, g:Y→Z and h:Z→W be functions. Then (h∘g)∘f=h∘(g∘f).

thm-composition-partial-converse.title: Partial converse for compositions
thm-composition-partial-converse.html:
Let f:X→Y and g:Y→Z be functions.

  1. If g∘f is injective, then f is injective.
  2. If g∘f is surjective, then g is surjective.

thm-composition-preserves.title: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity
thm-composition-preserves.html:
Let f:X→Y and g:Y→Z be functions.

  1. If f and g are injective, then g∘f is injective.
  2. If f and g are surjective, then g∘f is surjective.
  3. If f and g are bijective, then g∘f is bijective.

thm-conjugate-properties.title: Properties of Conjugation and Modulus
thm-conjugate-properties.html:
For all z,w∈C:

  1. z+w―=z―+w― and z――=z;
  2. zw―=z―w―;
  3. zz―=|z|2 and z+z―=2Rez;
  4. |zw|=|z||w| and |z―|=|z|.

thm-contrapositive-equivalent.title: Contrapositive equivalence
thm-contrapositive-equivalent.html: For all statements P and Q, the implication P⇒Q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬Q⇒¬P.

thm-de-moivre.title: De Moivre’s Formula
thm-de-moivre.html: For every θ∈R and every n∈N, (eiθ)n=einθ,that is,(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)n=cos⁡nθ+isin⁡nθ. Consequently (reiθ)n=rneinθ for every real r>0.

thm-de-morgan-logic.title: De Morgan’s laws for statements
thm-de-morgan-logic.html:
For all statements P and Q:

  1. ¬(P∧Q)≡¬P∨¬Q;
  2. ¬(P∨Q)≡¬P∧¬Q;
  3. ¬(P⇒Q)≡P∧¬Q.

thm-de-morgan-sets.title: De Morgan’s laws for sets
thm-de-morgan-sets.html:
Let A, B and C be sets. Then

  1. A∖(B∪C)=(A∖B)∩(A∖C);
  2. A∖(B∩C)=(A∖B)∪(A∖C).

In particular, if B,C⊆U, then (B∪C)c=Bc∩Cc and (B∩C)c=Bc∪Cc.

thm-degree-of-product.title: Degree of a product
thm-degree-of-product.html: Let F be a field and p,q∈F[x]. Then deg⁡(pq)=deg⁡p+deg⁡q. If p and q are non-zero, the leading coefficient of pq is the product of their leading coefficients.

thm-degree-of-sum.title: Degree of a sum
thm-degree-of-sum.html: Let F be a field and p,q∈F[x]. Then deg⁡(p+q)≤max(deg⁡p,deg⁡q), with equality whenever deg⁡p≠deg⁡q.

thm-distributive-sets.title: Distributive laws for sets
thm-distributive-sets.html:
Let A, B and C be sets. Then

  1. A∩(B∪C)=(A∩B)∪(A∩C);
  2. A∪(B∩C)=(A∪B)∩(A∪C).

thm-double-inclusion.title: Double inclusion
thm-double-inclusion.html: Let A and B be sets. Then A=B if and only if A⊆B and B⊆A.

thm-evaluation-respects-operations.title: Evaluation respects sums and products
thm-evaluation-respects-operations.html: Let F be a field, p,q∈F[x] and c∈F. Then (p+q)(c)=p(c)+q(c),(pq)(c)=p(c)q(c), and the constant polynomial a has value a at c.

thm-field-basic-properties.title: Basic Properties of Fields
thm-field-basic-properties.html:
Let F be a field and let a,b,c∈F.

  1. The element 0 in (F3) is unique, and the element 1 in (F7) is unique.
  2. (Cancellation) If a+b=a+c, then b=c. If ab=ac and a≠0, then b=c.
  3. The negative −a in (F4) is unique, and for a≠0 the inverse a−1 in (F8) is unique.
  4. 0⋅a=0.
  5. (−1)a=−a.
  6. If ab=0, then a=0 or b=0.

thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective.title: Injective iff surjective for finite sets of equal size
thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective.title_html: Injective iff surjective for finite sets of equal size
thm-finite-injective-iff-surjective.html: Let X and Y be finite sets with |X|=|Y|, and let f:X→Y. Then f is injective if and only if f is surjective. In that case f is bijective.

thm-fta-statement.title: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, Statement
thm-fta-statement.html: Let n≥1 and let a0,a1,…,an∈C with an≠0. Then there exists z∈C with anzn+an−1zn−1+⋯+a1z+a0=0.

thm-group-basic-properties.title: Basic properties of groups
thm-group-basic-properties.html:
Let G be a group and a,b,c∈G.

  1. The identity element of G is unique.
  2. The inverse of a is unique. We denote it by a−1.
  3. (a−1)−1=a and (ab)−1=b−1a−1.
  4. (Cancellation) If ab=ac, then b=c. If ba=ca, then b=c.

thm-homomorphism-basic-properties.title: Basic properties of homomorphisms
thm-homomorphism-basic-properties.html: Let φ:G→H be a homomorphism of groups. Then φ(eG)=eH, φ(a−1)=φ(a)−1 for every a∈G, and kerφ is a subgroup of G.

thm-induction.title: Principle of Mathematical Induction
thm-induction.html:
Let n0 be an integer, and for each integer n≥n0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose

  1. (base case) P(n0) is true, and
  2. (inductive step) for every integer n≥n0, if P(n) is true then P(n+1) is true.

Then P(n) is true for every integer n≥n0.

thm-inverse-matrix-properties.title: Properties of inverses
thm-inverse-matrix-properties.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. (Uniqueness) If B and B′ are both inverses of A, then B=B′. We write A−1 for the inverse of an invertible A.
  2. If A is invertible, then so is A−1, and (A−1)−1=A.
  3. If A and B are invertible, then so is AB, and (AB)−1=B−1A−1.
  4. If A is invertible, then so is AT, and (AT)−1=(A−1)T.
  5. If A is invertible and c∈F is non-zero, then cA is invertible, and (cA)−1=c−1A−1.
  6. (Cancellation) If A is invertible, then AX=AY implies X=Y for all X,Y∈Mn×p(F), and XA=YA implies X=Y for all X,Y∈Mp×n(F).
  7. (Solving) If A is invertible, then for every b∈Fn the equation Ax=b has exactly one solution x∈Fn, namely x=A−1b.

thm-inverse-of-composition.title: Inverse of a composition
thm-inverse-of-composition.html: Let f:X→Y and g:Y→Z be bijective. Then g∘f is bijective and (g∘f)−1=f−1∘g−1.

thm-left-inverse-iff-injective.title: Left inverses and injectivity
thm-left-inverse-iff-injective.html: Let f:X→Y with X non-empty. Then f has a left inverse if and only if f is injective.

thm-matrix-addition-properties.title: Properties of addition and scalar multiplication
thm-matrix-addition-properties.title_html: Properties of addition and scalar multiplication
thm-matrix-addition-properties.html:
Let A,B,C∈Mm×n(F) and c,d∈F. Then:

  1. A+B=B+A;
  2. (A+B)+C=A+(B+C);
  3. A+0=A;
  4. A+(−A)=0;
  5. c(A+B)=cA+cB and (c+d)A=cA+dA;
  6. (cd)A=c(dA) and 1A=A.

thm-matrix-multiplication-properties.title: Properties of matrix multiplication
thm-matrix-multiplication-properties.html:
Let c∈F, and let A,A′∈Mm×n(F), B,B′∈Mn×p(F) and C∈Mp×q(F). Then:

  1. (Associativity) (AB)C=A(BC);
  2. (Distributivity) A(B+B′)=AB+AB′ and (A+A′)B=AB+A′B;
  3. (Identity) ImA=A=AIn;
  4. (Scalars) c(AB)=(cA)B=A(cB);
  5. (Zero) 0ℓ×mA=0ℓ×n and A0n×r=0m×r for all ℓ,r≥1.

thm-matrix-times-vector-columns.title: A\x is a combination of the columns of A
thm-matrix-times-vector-columns.title_html: Ax is a combination of the columns of A
thm-matrix-times-vector-columns.html: Let A=(a1⋯an)∈Mm×n(F) with columns aj∈Fm, and let x=(x1,…,xn)∈Fn. Then Ax=x1a1+x2a2+⋯+xnan. In particular Aej=aj for each j. Similarly, if r1,…,rm are the rows of A and y=(y1⋯ym) is a row vector, then yA=y1r1+⋯+ymrm.

thm-partition.title: Equivalence relations and partitions
thm-partition.html:
Let X be a set.

  1. If ∼ is an equivalence relation on X, then the set of its equivalence classes is a partition of X.
  2. If P is a partition of X, then the relation “x∼Py if x and y lie in the same block” is an equivalence relation on X, and its equivalence classes are exactly the blocks of P.
  3. The two constructions undo each other: starting from ∼, the relation defined in (b) by the partition in (a) is ∼ again.

thm-polar-multiplication.title: Multiplication in Polar Form
thm-polar-multiplication.html: For all θ,φ∈R, eiθeiφ=ei(θ+φ). Consequently, if z=reiθ and w=seiφ with r,s>0, then zw=rsei(θ+φ).

thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties.title: Polynomials in one matrix
thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) and p,q∈F[x]. Then:

  1. AjAk=Aj+k for all j,k∈N;
  2. (p+q)(A)=p(A)+q(A) and (pq)(A)=p(A)q(A);
  3. p(A)q(A)=q(A)p(A).

thm-polynomial-ring-laws.title: Arithmetic in F[x]
thm-polynomial-ring-laws.title_html: Arithmetic in F[x]
thm-polynomial-ring-laws.html:
Let F be a field and p,q,r∈F[x]. Then:

  1. p+q=q+p and (p+q)+r=p+(q+r);
  2. p+0=p, and p+(−p)=0, where −p=∑(−ak)xk;
  3. pq=qp and (pq)r=p(qr);
  4. 1⋅p=p, where 1 is the constant polynomial (1,0,0,…);
  5. p(q+r)=pq+pr.

thm-right-inverse-iff-surjective.title: Right inverses and surjectivity
thm-right-inverse-iff-surjective.html: Let f:X→Y. Then f has a right inverse if and only if f is surjective.

thm-sqrt2-irrational.title: Irrationality of \sqrt{2}
thm-sqrt2-irrational.title_html: Irrationality of 2
thm-sqrt2-irrational.html: There is no rational number whose square is 2. That is, 2 is irrational.

thm-strong-induction.title: Strong induction
thm-strong-induction.html: Let n0 be an integer, and for each integer n≥n0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose that for every integer n≥n0, if P(k) is true for all integers k with n0≤k<n, then P(n) is true. Then P(n) is true for every integer n≥n0.

thm-subgroup-test.title: Subgroup test
thm-subgroup-test.html: Let G be a group and H⊆G. Then H is a subgroup of G if and only if H≠∅ and ab−1∈H for all a,b∈H.

thm-three-views-of-product.title: Three views of a product
thm-three-views-of-product.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F), and write B=(b1⋯bp) with columns bk∈Fn. Then:

  1. (Entries) (AB)ik=∑j=1naijbjk for all i,k;
  2. (Columns) the k-th column of AB is Abk, that is, AB=(Ab1Ab2⋯Abp);
  3. (Rows) the i-th row of AB is (row i of A)B.

thm-trace-properties.title: Properties of the trace
thm-trace-properties.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) and c∈F. Then:

  1. tr(A+B)=trA+trB and tr(cA)=ctrA;
  2. tr(AT)=trA;
  3. tr(AB)=tr(BA). More generally, this holds for all A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F), where AB is m×m and BA is n×n.

thm-transpose-properties.title: Properties of the transpose
thm-transpose-properties.html:
Let c∈F. For matrices of sizes for which each expression is defined:

  1. (AT)T=A;
  2. (A+B)T=AT+BT;
  3. (cA)T=cAT;
  4. (AB)T=BTAT for A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×p(F).

thm-transpositions-generate.title: Transpositions generate S_n
thm-transpositions-generate.title_html: Transpositions generate Sn
thm-transpositions-generate.html: Let n≥2. Every permutation in Sn is a product of transpositions.

thm-two-by-two-inverse.title: Inverse of a 2 \times 2 matrix
thm-two-by-two-inverse.title_html: Inverse of a 2×2 matrix
thm-two-by-two-inverse.html: Let A=(abcd)∈M2(F). Then A is invertible if and only if ad−bc≠0. In that case, A−1=1ad−bc(d−b−ca).

thm-well-defined-on-quotient.title: Functions on a quotient
thm-well-defined-on-quotient.html:
Let ∼ be an equivalence relation on X, let π:X→X/∼ be the quotient map, and let f:X→Y be a function.

  1. If f(a)=f(b) whenever a∼b, then there is exactly one function f¯:X/∼→Y with f¯([x])=f(x) for every x∈X, that is, f¯∘π=f.
  2. Conversely, if some function f¯:X/∼→Y satisfies f¯∘π=f, then f(a)=f(b) whenever a∼b.

thm-well-ordering.title: Well-Ordering Principle
thm-well-ordering.html: Every non-empty collection of natural numbers has a least element: an element m of the collection with m≤s for every s in the collection.

thm-zp-field-iff-prime.title: \nZ/n\nZ Is a Field Exactly for Prime n
thm-zp-field-iff-prime.title_html: Z/nZ Is a Field Exactly for Prime n
thm-zp-field-iff-prime.html: Let n≥2 be an integer. Then Z/nZ is a field if and only if n is prime.
